subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The rise in cohabitation is best interpreted as evidence of which broad trend?
options: The growing diversity of family and household forms
The return of the extended family
questions.explain: Increasing cohabitation reflects greater diversity and changing attitudes towards marriage.

questions.q: Which factor is most commonly cited as contributing to the long-term rise in the divorce rate?
options: The 1969 Divorce Reform Act making divorce easier
questions.explain: Legal changes such as the 1969 Divorce Reform Act, alongside secularisation and changing attitudes, increased divorce.

questions.q: Willmott and Young's thesis that the family is becoming more equal with shared roles is known as the:
questions.explain: Willmott and Young argued the modern family is becoming more 'symmetrical', with conjugal roles more equally shared.

questions.q: Parsons argued that which family type best 'fits' the needs of modern industrial society?
questions.explain: Parsons claimed the geographically and socially mobile nuclear family fits the needs of industrial society.

questions.q: Which feminist perspective sees the family as the main site of women's oppression and patriarchy, sometimes advocating separatism?
questions.explain: Radical feminists argue the family and marriage are key institutions of patriarchal oppression.

questions.q: In Engels' Marxist account, the monogamous nuclear family emerged primarily to serve which function?
options: The reduction of the birth rate
The inheritance of private property through legitimate heirs
questions.explain: Engels argued monogamy arose to ensure men could pass private property to their legitimate biological heirs.

questions.q: Marxists are critical of the functionalist view of social policy because they argue policies:
options: Have no effect on family life
Tend to serve the interests of capitalism rather than families equally
questions.explain: Marxists argue social policy ultimately props up capitalism rather than neutrally helping all families.

questions.q: A 'reconstituted' (blended) family is one that:
options: Is headed by a single parent
Consists of a couple with no children
Is formed when partners with children from previous relationships join together
questions.explain: A reconstituted or step-family forms when at least one partner brings a child from a previous relationship.

questions.q: The 'cereal-packet image' of the family refers to:
options: The Marxist view of the family
The idealised conventional nuclear family promoted in adverts and media
questions.explain: Leach's 'cereal-packet family' is the idealised nuclear family image, which most households no longer match.

questions.q: Donzelot's view of social policy emphasises that the state exercises which over families?
questions.explain: Donzelot argues social policy enables state surveillance and the 'policing of families', especially the poor.

questions.q: Hakim's 'preference theory' argues that women's varied family and work patterns are best explained by:
options: Women's own rational choices and preferences
questions.explain: Hakim argues women actively choose their work-family balance according to personal preferences, downplaying structural constraints.

questions.q: According to Parsons, what are the two 'irreducible functions' of the family in modern industrial society?
options: Primary socialisation and the stabilisation of adult personalities
questions.explain: Parsons argued the family retains primary socialisation of children and the stabilisation of adult personalities (the 'warm bath' theory).

questions.q: Philippe Aries is associated with which claim about childhood?
options: The position of children has worsened over time
Childhood is a social construction that did not exist as today in the Middle Ages
questions.explain: Aries argued childhood as a distinct, protected status is a relatively recent social construction.

questions.q: Postman and others argue childhood is now disappearing or changing, partly due to:
options: The decline of the nuclear family
Children's growing access to the adult world via media
questions.explain: Postman argued the boundary between childhood and adulthood is blurring, partly through media access ('the disappearance of childhood').

questions.q: The conflict view of childhood (e.g. Firestone) argues that protections such as compulsory schooling actually represent:
options: Forms of control and oppression of children
A genuine improvement in children's welfare
A response to the ageing population
questions.explain: Conflict theorists argue 'protections' are really controls that segregate and oppress children rather than benefit them.

questions.q: The 'march of progress' view of childhood argues that:
options: The position of children has steadily improved over time
Childhood is increasingly controlled and policed
questions.explain: The march of progress view holds that children's lives have steadily improved and they are more valued and protected.

questions.q: Postmodernists such as Stacey argue that contemporary family life is best described as which of the following?
options: Diverse, fragmented and a matter of individual choice
questions.explain: Postmodernists argue family forms are now diverse and chosen, reflecting greater individual freedom and fragmentation.

questions.q: The Rapoports identified several types of family diversity. Which of the following was one of their five types?
questions.explain: The Rapoports' five types include organisational, cultural, social class, life-stage and generational (cohort) diversity.

questions.q: Which sociologist critiqued Willmott and Young's symmetrical-family claim, finding men's domestic 'help' was greatly exaggerated?
questions.explain: Oakley argued Willmott and Young's evidence was flimsy and that women still did the vast majority of housework.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key reason given for the long-term decline in the birth rate?
options: Falling infant mortality and the changing position of women
questions.explain: Lower infant mortality and changes such as women's education and careers help explain the long-term fall in the birth rate.

questions.q: The 'total fertility rate' (TFR) refers to:
options: The number of live births per 1,000 of the population per year
The number of deaths per 1,000 per year
The average number of children women will have during their childbearing years
The proportion of the population over 65
questions.explain: The TFR is the average number of children a woman will have over her fertile years; the UK's has fallen long-term.

questions.q: The 'beanpole family' that may result from demographic change is best described as:
options: A multi-generational but narrow family with few members per generation
questions.explain: The beanpole family is extended vertically (several living generations) but narrow, with fewer children per generation.

questions.q: The 'ageing population' refers to which demographic trend?
options: An increase in the average age of the population
questions.explain: An ageing population means the average age is rising, driven by longer life expectancy and a falling birth rate.

questions.q: The New Right perspective on the family is best characterised by which view?
options: The family serves capitalism by exploiting women
The traditional patriarchal nuclear family is the bedrock of a stable society
The nuclear family is outdated and oppressive
Family diversity should be celebrated equally
questions.explain: The New Right (e.g. Charles Murray) sees the conventional nuclear family as natural and best, blaming lone parenthood for social problems.

questions.q: Duncombe and Marsden's concept of the 'triple shift' adds which third element to paid work and housework?
questions.explain: The triple shift adds 'emotion work' — managing the emotional wellbeing of the family — to paid and domestic work.

questions.q: Which functionalist sociologist identified four essential functions of the family: sexual, reproductive, economic and educational?
questions.explain: Murdock argued the nuclear family is universal because it performs four essential functions for society.

questions.q: Which Marxist sociologist argued the family is a haven where workers can be 'themselves' but also reproduces capitalist values like obedience?
questions.explain: Zaretsky argued the family cushions workers but ultimately serves capitalism by reproducing labour and absorbing discontent.

questions.q: The idea that working women perform paid work AND most domestic labour is referred to as the:
questions.explain: The dual burden describes women doing both paid employment and the bulk of unpaid housework.

questions.q: Marxist feminists such as Margaret Benston argue that women's unpaid domestic labour primarily benefits whom?
options: Capitalism, by reproducing labour power cheaply
questions.explain: Marxist feminists argue women's unpaid domestic labour reproduces and maintains the labour force at no cost to capitalism.

questions.q: Which feminist perspective criticises others for assuming all women share the same experience, stressing variation by ethnicity, class and sexuality?
questions.explain: Difference feminists argue women's family experiences differ by ethnicity, class and sexuality, rejecting a single account.
